opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it comes from a mix of curiosity and a bit of restlessness about where the field has been going. For the last several years, so much of the energy in AI has gone into making models bigger and better at the things we already know how to measure: benchmarks, chat quality, coding. Those are important, but I've always been more drawn to the questions where we don't yet know the answer, where even humans are still struggling. Science is exactly that kind of space.

What excites me personally is the possibility that AI could help us discover something genuinely new, not just retrieve or remix what's already in the training data. That's a very different bar. When a model solves a math problem that's already on the internet somewhere, it's hard to tell how much is reasoning and how much is pattern matching. But if it can help form a hypothesis that turns out to be true and that nobody had written down before, that tells you something deeper about intelligence, both artificial and human.

There's also a humanistic side to it for me. I care a lot about AI being something that broadly benefits people, not just a technology that concentrates power or capability in a few places. Science, when it goes well, is one of humanity's most collective and generous enterprises. Medicine, materials, climate, basic understanding of the world. If AI can accelerate that, and make it more accessible to smaller labs and researchers who don't have huge resources, that feels like a really meaningful direction.

And honestly, it's intellectually humbling. Working on AI for science forces you to confront what these models can't do: where they're overconfident, where they lack real understanding, where common sense or careful reasoning breaks down. I've spent a lot of my career thinking about those gaps, and science is a place where the gaps matter in very concrete ways. So it's both exciting and a little scary, and I think that combination is usually a sign you're working on something worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI for science should discover something genuinely new rather than retrieve or remix training data, including forming a true hypothesis nobody had written down before. This communicates reaching beyond knowledge reflected in internet data.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, this is something I've been thinking about a lot. You know, for most of my career I've worked on language and commonsense reasoning, and the thing that always fascinated me was this gap between what models can memorize and what they can actually figure out. And science is kind of the ultimate test of that, right? Because the whole point of science is to discover something that isn't already written down anywhere.

So part of my excitement is intellectual. If you want to know whether these models can really reason, as opposed to just pattern-matching against the internet, science is where you find out. You can't fake a new theorem or a new material. Either it works or it doesn't. And I find that really refreshing after years of benchmarks where you're never quite sure whether the model saw the answer during training.

But honestly, the bigger reason is more personal. There are so many problems, in biology, in climate, in math, where the bottleneck isn't lack of data or lack of compute, it's that there just aren't enough people who can hold all of the relevant knowledge in their head at once and make the connections. And I think AI can genuinely help there, not by replacing scientists, but by being this tireless collaborator that reads everything and proposes ideas, some of which are wrong, some of which are weird, and a few of which turn out to be exactly the thing nobody thought to try.

And I'll admit, there's also a bit of a contrarian streak in me. A lot of the field right now is very focused on scaling and on products, and I think the harder, more interesting question is whether we can build systems that are actually creative in a disciplined way. Can they form a hypothesis, be skeptical of it, test it, and change their mind? That's not just a science question, that's a question about what intelligence is. So for me AI for science is where my curiosity about reasoning and my desire to do something that matters kind of meet in the same place.

r001.rationale: The candidate says science is about discovering something “isn't already written down anywhere” and contrasts genuine reasoning with pattern matching against the internet, communicating that AI for science must reach beyond knowledge reflected in internet data.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility that AI could help us discover something that we don’t already know. A lot of what we do with language models is train them on human knowledge and ask them to reproduce or synthesize it. That’s useful, but science asks us to go further—to generate new hypotheses and test them against the world.

And that creates a really interesting challenge for AI. Can it help us see connections that we’ve missed? Can it reason through an unfamiliar problem, rather than give an answer that sounds plausible? Scientific discovery gives us a way to ground those questions in evidence.

For me, it’s also about the potential benefit. If we can build AI that helps scientists tackle difficult problems, we can expand what people are able to discover. That’s a compelling direction both for understanding intelligence and for making it useful.

r001.rationale: The response says AI for science should generate new hypotheses and discover things beyond what is already known. It does not identify internet data as the source of the human knowledge that AI must go beyond.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility that AI could help us discover something we don’t yet know. A lot of what we do with AI is about learning from existing human knowledge. But in science, there’s an opportunity to go beyond that—to help us generate new hypotheses, explore possibilities we might otherwise miss, and test our understanding of the world.

And I think that creates a really interesting challenge for AI itself. Can it reason about something unfamiliar? Can it recognize when its explanation is wrong and revise it based on evidence? For me, that combination—advancing AI while helping people make scientific discoveries—is really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says AI for science can go beyond existing human knowledge, but it does not identify that this knowledge is reflected in internet data.
